_note: Events from Reggie, Biscuit and Mochi, 2026-10-23. THE GREAT TRASH CAN MYSTERY is Dr. O's own text, verbatim, with only her name changed to the {name} token. The other five are written out in full in her style for her to read and change: Reggie starts, Biscuit takes over, Mochi cuts in, each remembers it differently, and the day ends with a quiet scene and Mochi's smallest word. Facts to check are in facts.

beats.text:
"OH OH OH!"
"You're here!"
"Okay, so you know how sometimes destiny happens?"
Mochi looked up from his nap.
"It doesn't."
"It DOES."
I ignored him because this is my story.
Anyway.
It started at 9:14 in the morning.
Or maybe 9:15.
Definitely morning.
Biscuit and I were conducting neighborhood security operations.
"Sniffing," Mochi said.
We were conducting security operations when I detected something.
Something strange.
Something important.
Something magnificent.
I stopped so suddenly Biscuit walked right into me.
"What is it, sugar?" she asked.
I raised my nose to the wind.
"There."
"What?"
"That."
"What is 'that'?"
"The smell."
Everything went silent.
Even the birds.
We all smelled it.
A smell so incredible.
So mysterious.
So powerful.
That we knew immediately:
An adventure had begun.

Now {name}.
Let me tell this proper.
It was a lovely morning.
Blue sky.
Gentle breeze.
The kind of day that makes you grateful to have paws.
The three of us were enjoying a pleasant stroll when Reggie froze.
Not unusual.
Reggie has stopped for dandelions.
Clouds.
A particularly ambitious ant.
So naturally I thought nothing of it.
Then I saw his face.
Well.
His eyes got big.
His ears perked up.
And I knew.
Trouble had arrived.
"Do you smell that?" asked Reggie.
And honey...
I surely did.
The breeze carried a scent so fascinating that I cannot adequately describe it.
It had notes of barbecue.
A hint of pizza.
Possibly cheese.
And maybe...
Maybe...
Hot dogs.
The smell drifted from a large green trash can behind a fence.
A trash can, {name}.
A trash can with stories to tell.
Trash can.

We approached carefully.
Very carefully.
Like explorers.
Or detectives.
Or detective explorers.
The smell got stronger.
Biscuit gasped.
I gasped.
Mochi didn't gasp because Mochi never gasps.
He barely participates.
"It could be anything," I whispered.
"Probably trash," said Mochi.
"It could be treasure."
"Trash."
"It could be evidence."
"Trash."
"It could be an international conspiracy."
"Trash."
Honestly I don't know why he's like that.

Now I believe every mystery deserves respect.
So I examined the situation.
The fence was tall.
The gate was closed.
The trash can sat beyond our reach like some distant green monument.
And that smell...
Mercy.
That smell was singing.
Calling.
Inviting.
Promising answers.
Reggie looked at me.
I looked at Reggie.
We both looked at Mochi.
Mochi looked tired.
I was tired.

Then inspiration struck.
A plan.
A brilliant plan.
One of my best.
Top ten easily.
Maybe top five.
"Boost me."
Biscuit squinted.
"I don't know about that."
"We need answers."
"We do not."
"We absolutely do."
Mochi sighed.
That should have been our warning.

Now when Mochi sighs like that, one of two things is happening.
Either trouble is coming.
Or trouble is already here.
This turned out to be both.

Biscuit gave me a boost.
I climbed onto a flower pot.
Then onto a decorative rock.
Then onto a garden statue.
Then...
The statue tilted.
The flower pot tipped.
The rock moved.
And suddenly I discovered gravity.
Again.

What happened next occurred very quickly.
Reggie fell.
The flower pot fell.
The statue fell.
A watering can fell.
Three rakes became involved for reasons still unclear.
He fell.

I DID NOT FALL.
I strategically descended.
Unexpectedly.
At speed.

The commotion brought a human outside.
Now normally that might be concerning.
But this lovely person simply walked over to the trash can.
Opened the lid.
And revealed the source of our mystery.

You know what was inside?
You'll never guess.
Never.
Not in a million years.
Pizza.

YES.
Pizza.
An entire pizza box.
The smell of legends.
The aroma of champions.
The treasure at the end of our journey.

And there we stood.
Three explorers.
One mystery solved.
One friendship strengthened.
One flower pot sacrificed in the pursuit of truth.
A very successful morning all around.

We found pizza.
Reggie fell.
The end.

episodes.evening:
Reggie stretched across the living room.
"That was a great adventure."
"It was a trash can."
"It was a mystery."
"It was a trash can."
"It was BOTH."
Biscuit smiled.
"I think the real treasure was spending the day together."
Silence.
Mochi looked at both of them.
Then gave the smallest nod.
"Yeah."
Reggie grinned.
Biscuit smiled.
And somehow that one word felt a lot bigger than all the others.

card.front: The Great Trash Can Mystery: one pizza box
card.back: Reggie: It was BOTH. Biscuit: The real treasure was the day together. Mochi: Yeah.

beats.text:
"OH OH OH!"
"You have terrible timing!"
"The squirrel situation JUST escalated."
Mochi opened one eye.
"It didn't."
"It DID."
I ignored him, because this is my story.
Anyway.
It was 7:42 in the morning.
Or 7:43.
Definitely morning.
Biscuit and I were out in the yard conducting a perimeter check.
"Sniffing," Mochi said.
We were conducting the check when I saw him.
On the fence.
Right there on top of our fence.
A squirrel.
Sitting there like he paid for it.

Well hello there, sweet pea. Come on in, {name}.
I've got a story for you, and I'll tell you now, it takes a little explainin'.
It was a lovely morning.
Dew on the grass.
The sun just coming up over the neighbors' roof.
A mockingbird somewhere running through every song he knew.
The whole yard smelled like wet cedar and cut grass and, baby, just a little bit of bacon from the neighbors' kitchen.
And I remember thinkin', now this is the kind of morning that makes a dog grateful for her whiskers.
Then Reggie went stiff as a board.
Not unusual.
Reggie has gone stiff for a leaf.
A cloud.
A particularly dramatic sneeze.
But this time, honey, he had good reason.
Squirrel.

He was eating something.
Something round.
Something small.
Something he clearly stole from our own yard.
And he looked at me.
Straight at me.
And he chewed slower.
"Slower," Biscuit said.
Slower, on PURPOSE.
That is a declaration of war.
I told Biscuit, "I'm going in."
"Reggie."
"I'm going in."
"Sugar, you are not going in."
"I am a professional."
Mochi sighed.
That should have been our warning.

Now when Mochi sighs like that, one of two things is happenin'.
Either trouble is comin'.
Or trouble is already here.
This was both.
Because Reggie went in.
Sprinted across that yard like a golden comet.
Ears flyin'.
Tongue flyin'.
One whole paw off the ground in a manner that I would call ambitious.
And that squirrel, baby, did not move.
Not one inch.
He just watched Reggie come, calm as a deacon, until Reggie was right at the base of the fence.
And then he went up.
Straight up.
And across.
And onto the wire.
And Reggie ran the entire length of that fence, barkin', and the squirrel walked above him on the wire, like a tightrope walker, takin' his time.
Wire. No dogs.

It was a BATTLE.
A real one.
He threw an acorn at me.
"He dropped it," Mochi said.
He THREW it.
It bounced off my head.
On purpose.
I defended the yard.
I held the line.
I want that on the record.

Now I believe every dispute deserves a fair hearing.
So I stepped in.
Calm.
Dignified.
I said, "Mister Squirrel, let's all take a breath."
He looked at me.
I looked at him.
I offered terms.
I said, "We'll leave you the walnut tree, and you leave us the yard."
He said nothin'.
I offered a biscuit.
I dropped a whole biscuit at the foot of that fence, baby.
My good one.
And you know what that squirrel did?
He came down, took the biscuit, and went right back up the wire.
With my biscuit.
The talks, sugar, did not go well.
Negotiation failed.

We didn't lose.
Technically.
We were out-maneuvered.
By a professional.
With a very good tail.
Squirrel won.
I will not have that in my story.

episodes.evening:
That night the three of them lay in a heap on the kitchen floor.
Reggie stared at the ceiling.
"That was a battle."
"Negotiation failed," said Biscuit.
Mochi did not open his eyes.
"Squirrel won."
Reggie was quiet for a long time.
"Okay," he said.
"Technically."
Biscuit sighed and rested her chin on his back.
"I think the best part of the whole morning was the three of us being out there together."
Silence.
Mochi, without opening his eyes, shifted until he was pressed against Reggie's side.
"Yeah."
Reggie smiled at the ceiling.
And somewhere outside, on the wire, a squirrel ate a biscuit in the dark.

card.front: The Great Squirrel Incident: negotiations failed
card.back: Reggie: BATTLE. Biscuit: Negotiation failed. Mochi: Squirrel won. Yeah.

facts: VERIFY: squirrels run along wires and fences, where a dog cannot follow

beats.text:
"OH OH OH, YOU'RE HERE!"
"Okay, so you know how sometimes the universe hands you a gift?"
Mochi looked up from his nap.
"It doesn't."
"It DOES."
I ignored him because this is my story.
Anyway.
It was after the big storm.
The wind had been howling all night.
And the next morning, the park looked different.
Branches everywhere.
Leaves everywhere.
A whole new world.
And there, in the middle of the grass, lay the stick.
THE stick.
The biggest stick we had ever seen.
I stopped so suddenly Biscuit walked into me.
"What is it, sugar?"
"There."
"What?"
"That."

Now {name}, let me tell this proper.
It was a gorgeous morning after a night of weather.
The grass was soaked and cold under the paws.
The air smelled like rain and torn leaves and sawdust, and somewhere in the distance, a man was dragging a branch to the curb.
The three of us were takin' a stroll when Reggie froze.
And honey, he got that look.
That look he gets when he's found his purpose.
I turned my head, and there it was.
A good six feet of oak.
Straight as a preacher.
With bark, baby, that had character.
It looked like it had been waitin' there since the Flood.
Stick.

It was destiny.
Chosen by fate.
It was lying there in the leaves, and it was waiting for ME.
I walked up to it very slowly.
With respect.
I took one end in my mouth.
It was heavy.
Majestic.
It smelled like thunder.
Biscuit said, "Reggie, honey, that's awfully big."
"I can handle it."
"It's taller than you."
"I can handle it."
"It's taller than all of us."
Mochi said, "Stick."
He says that a lot.
It's not helpful.

Now I want you to understand somethin', {name}.
I've seen a lot of sticks.
I've seen small sticks, and crooked sticks, and a very sad stick once that had been chewed by a beagle.
But this one?
This one had remarkable craftsmanship.
Nature does not make a stick like that twice.
So I did what any lady would do.
I stepped back, and I let Reggie carry it.
Because some things, baby, a friend has to do on their own.
Too long.

I carried it the whole way.
Nearly the whole way.
Across the grass.
Past the fountain.
Past a very impressed pigeon.
Down the sidewalk.
Everybody stopped.
A man on a bike said, "Look at that dog."
I nodded.
Biscuit walked beside me with her head held high.
Mochi walked behind us, sighing at regular intervals.
It was the best walk of my life.
And then we got to the gate.

Now the gate to our yard, {name}, is a perfectly good gate.
It has been a perfectly good gate for years.
It opens, and it closes, and it has never once given anyone a problem.
But that stick had its own opinions.
Reggie walked up to it.
The stick did not.
It went sideways.
There was a clunk.
Reggie stopped, and the stick stopped, and there we stood, three dogs and a branch, wedged across the gate like a very serious toll booth.
Sideways.

I tried everything.
I tried pulling.
I tried pushing.
I tried turning my head.
I tried turning the stick.
I tried going through backwards.
I've never done that before.
It didn't work.
But I want you to know, I never let go.
Not once.

Eventually a human came out to see what all the fuss was about.
A lovely person.
Patient.
She looked at Reggie.
She looked at the stick.
She looked at the gate.
And then, baby, she did the kindest thing I've ever seen a human do.
She lifted that big old stick, turned it just so, and carried it into the yard.
Then she leaned it against the fence like a monument.
And she went back inside, shakin' her head, smilin'.
Finally.

It's still there.
It's the greatest thing in the whole yard.
You can see it from the kitchen window.

episodes.evening:
That evening the yard turned gold.
Reggie lay on the grass with his chin on his paws, looking at the stick.
"It was a good stick."
"Remarkable craftsmanship," said Biscuit.
Mochi did not lift his head.
"Stick."
Reggie smiled.
"The best one."
Biscuit leaned her shoulder against his.
"I think the real treasure was walking it home together."
Silence.
Mochi got up, walked slowly across the grass, and lay down on the other side of the stick, close enough that his nose touched the bark.
"Good stick," he said.
Reggie grinned.
Biscuit smiled.
And somehow that one little word felt like a medal.

card.front: The Stick of Destiny: too wide for the gate
card.back: Reggie: Chosen by fate. Biscuit: Remarkable craftsmanship. Mochi: Stick. Good stick.

beats.text:
"OKAY, OKAY, OKAY!"
"You're here!"
"Do you know what the ocean does?"
Mochi looked up from the back seat.
"Wets."
"It LEAVES."
I ignored him because this is my story.
Anyway.
We got out of the car and the sea was gone.
Gone!
The whole bottom of the ocean was just lying there.
Sand as far as I could see.
Shiny.
Cold.
Full of mysteries.
Biscuit said, "Reggie, that's low tide."
I said, "It's a miracle."
And then I smelled it.
Something moving.
Something clever.
Something with a plan.

Well hello there, sweet pea. Come on in, {name}.
I've got a story for you.
It was the loveliest afternoon at the shore.
The gulls were hollerin' up a storm.
The air tasted like salt and seaweed and sunscreen and somebody's fried clams, and the sand was hard and cold and shinin', like the whole beach had just been polished.
Little pools of water everywhere the tide had left behind.
And Reggie, lord love him, dropped his nose to the ground and started tracking.
Slow.
Serious.
Like a detective in a picture show.
I said, "Honey, what is it?"
He said, "Crab."
And I thought, well now.
Crab. Maybe.

It was a CRAB.
A big one.
A crab with a plan.
I followed it for ten minutes.
Ten whole minutes.
Across the sand.
Around a rock.
Over a very tricky patch of seaweed.
It zigged.
I zagged.
It paused.
I paused.
We understood each other.
Biscuit followed behind me narrating everything.
Mochi followed behind her sighing.
I could hear the whole pack.

Meanwhile, {name}, Mochi had wandered off.
Said he came for the car ride and nothing more.
But I looked back, and that dignified bulldog was standing in a tide pool, up to his belly, in the cold water.
Looking out at the horizon.
With the saddest, most peaceful look.
I said, "Mochi, are you all right?"
And he said...
This is fine.

Honey, I have never been so proud.
That dog stood in the ocean for twenty minutes and did not say another word.

Meanwhile I had cornered the crab.
Behind a rock.
It wasn't moving.
It was waiting.
It was clever.
I crept closer.
My heart was pounding.
I leaned in.
I pounced.
And Biscuit said, "Reggie."
And I looked down.
And it was a shoe.
Shoe.

It was a DECOY shoe.
That is what I said at the time.
And I stand by it.
Somebody put that shoe there to confuse me.
A professional.
With excellent timing.

I want to say, {name}, I did not laugh.
Not out loud.
Not at first.
But the way Reggie looked at that shoe, with such dignity, like it had personally let him down, why baby, I laughed so hard I had to lie in the sand.
And the gulls laughed.
I swear they did.
And then the humans called out the word ice cream.
And we all ran.
Even Mochi.
Who had been in the water for twenty minutes.
And never mentioned it again.
Tide comes back.

episodes.evening:
In the car on the way home, the sun was low and the windows were fogged.
Reggie lay across the back seat with sand in his ears.
"That was a great adventure."
"It was a shoe," said Mochi.
"It was a decoy."
"It was a shoe."
"It was BOTH."
Biscuit laughed softly.
"I think the best part of the whole day was having the beach all to ourselves, the three of us."
Silence.
Mochi turned from the window.
He looked at Reggie, sound asleep with his head on Biscuit's paw.
Then he looked at Biscuit.
"Good day," he said.
Biscuit smiled.
Reggie, still asleep, wagged his tail.
And the sea, a mile behind them, began to come back in.

card.front: The beach at low tide: one crab, allegedly a shoe
card.back: Reggie: Decoy shoe. Biscuit: Best day of my life. Mochi: Shoe. Good day.

facts: At low tide the sea pulls back and leaves tide pools in the sand

beats.text:
"YOU'RE HERE!"
"You will NOT believe where the floor went."
Mochi looked up from the bench.
"Moved."
"It WENT."
I ignored him because this is my story.
Anyway.
We got in the car.
We drove.
And then we drove onto a BOAT.
Do you understand what I'm telling you?
A road that floats.
My first one.
I've been alive for years and nobody ever told me there were roads on the water.
We parked.
The humans opened the doors.
And I smelled the sea.

Well hello there, {name}. Come on in, have a seat.
I've got a story for you, and I do not mind sayin', it was the grandest thing.
The whole deck hummed under our paws.
A low, steady hum that I could feel in my teeth.
Salt wind blowin' across the rail.
A little diesel.
Gulls hangin' in the air like they were on strings.
And somewhere three rows over, baby, somebody's french fries.
I could have found those with my eyes closed.
We climbed up to the top deck, the three of us, with our humans.
And Reggie walked to the rail like he owned the sea.
Wet.

I stood there like a captain.
Ears back.
Nose up.
The wind in my face.
I surveyed the ocean.
It was very big.
And I thought, this is what freedom smells like.
And then I noticed her.

There was a woman on that deck, {name}, who was holdin' on to the rail so tight her knuckles were white.
Pale as milk.
Lookin' straight ahead and breathin' real slow.
Reggie saw her before I did.
He always does.
He reads people, that boy.
It's a gift.
And he walked over to her, quiet, and he sat down against her leg.
Didn't say a word.
Just leaned.
He leaned.

I SAVED her.
I want that on the record.
I leaned on her leg for the entire crossing.
Forty-five minutes.
I didn't move.
My leg fell asleep.
I didn't care.
She put her hand on my head and she stopped shaking.
That's what I do.
It's my job.

It was the sweetest thing, {name}.
She said, "Good boy."
Over and over.
And Reggie looked up at her like she'd handed him the moon.
Now, in the meantime, I'll tell you what became of Mochi.
He took one step onto that deck, and the floor moved.
Just a little.
Just a swell.
And that dignified bulldog sat down flat in the middle of the walkway and refused to go any farther.
He announced he would be filing a formal complaint.
Floor moved.

He said that the whole time.
"Floor moved."
"Floor moved."
It's a BOAT.
It's SUPPOSED to move.
Not floors.

And then, {name}, we came into the harbor.
The sun was settin' behind the hills, and the water was gold, and a big old bell was ringin' somewhere.
The engine hum slowed.
The deck stopped movin'.
And Mochi stood up, shook himself off, and walked right off that boat like nothing had happened.
And the woman at the rail let go of her breath, and she scratched Reggie behind the ears, and said, "Thank you."
And Reggie wagged so hard he knocked his own self over.

episodes.evening:
That night the three of them lay in a pile on the living room rug, still smelling faintly of salt.
"My first boat," Reggie said, to nobody.
"The floor moved," said Mochi.
"It did," said Biscuit.
Mochi sighed.
"Wasn't bad."
Biscuit laughed.
"I think the best part was having all three of us on that deck, together."
Silence.
Reggie was already half asleep.
Mochi looked at him for a long moment.
Then he shifted over and put his chin gently on Reggie's back.
"Yeah," he said.
And out in the dark, far away, the ferry rocked softly at its dock, humming to itself.

card.front: The ferry: a road that floats, officially
card.back: Reggie: I saved a human. Biscuit: The floor MOVED. Mochi: Floor moved. Wasn't bad.

facts: A ferry carries people and cars across water
Dogs can feel vibration through their paws

beats.text:
"OKAY, OKAY, OKAY!"
"You're here!"
"Do you know what a parking lot full of smells is?"
Mochi looked up from the shade.
"Market."
"It's a MIRACLE."
I ignored him because this is my story.
Anyway.
It was Saturday.
Or maybe Sunday.
Definitely a weekend.
The humans put on our leashes and said the word market.
And I didn't know what that meant.
But my whole body knew.
We turned the corner.
And there it was.
Tents.
Tables.
Baskets.
And the SMELL.
I stopped so suddenly Biscuit walked right into me.
"What is it, sugar?"
"Everything."

Well hello there, sweet pea. Come on in, {name}.
I've got a story for you, and it's a sweet one.
Peaches, baby.
Peaches, and warm bread, and a man fryin' onions in a pan the size of a wagon wheel, and a lady with honey you could smell from the car.
A farmers market is the whole world at nose height.
Every table, right at the level of my nose.
Cheese.
Tomatoes.
Cinnamon.
Basil.
A bucket of flowers somebody had cut that morning, still wet.
I thought I'd gone to heaven, and the Lord had put it all out on folding tables.
Samples.

Mochi found the cheese.
A lady gave him a piece.
A tiny one.
And he pretended he didn't care.
He said, "Fine."
And then he followed her for three stalls.
I saw it.
Biscuit saw it.
The cheese lady saw it.
He knows we saw it.
And he still pretends.
Acceptable.

Meanwhile, {name}, Reggie was workin'.
I could tell by his ears.
He'd spotted a table at the end of the row.
A little wooden table with a hand-painted sign and a crate of the prettiest peaches you ever saw.
But no customers.
And behind that table, a young woman, leanin' on her elbows, with her shoulders down and her eyes on the sidewalk.
Lord, you could tell.
She was havin' a slow mornin'.
The kind where you start to wonder if you ought to be there at all.

I saw her.
And I knew.
That table needed me.
I walked right up.
I sat down in front of it.
Perfectly still.
And I looked up at her.
Just looked.
I used the eyes.
The eyes.

Now I have watched that dog use those eyes on a mailman, a plumber, and a priest.
But I have never seen them work like that.
She looked down.
She smiled.
She came around the table and knelt down and said, "Well, hello there."
And Reggie put his paw on her knee.
And then, {name}, a lady stopped to pet him.
And she looked at the peaches.
And then her husband stopped.
And then two kids with sticky hands.
And a man in a hat.
And an old woman with a cane who said, "These smell like my grandmother's kitchen."
Before I knew it, baby, there was a line.

SIX people.
I counted.
Six people stopped.
She sold every peach.
Every single one.
The crate was EMPTY.
She looked at me like I was a hero.
Which I am.
I just don't like to say.
He says it.

She tucked a peach into her apron.
She got down on one knee and she held it out, and she said, "This one's for the best salesman in the market."
And Reggie, my sweet fool, took it so gently, like it was made of glass.
And carried it the whole way home in his mouth.
And never ate it.
It sat in the middle of the kitchen floor until bedtime.
Like a trophy.

episodes.evening:
That night Reggie told it again at dinner, to the humans, who did not understand a single word.
Biscuit narrated over him.
Mochi ate quietly, in his corner, and then looked up.
"Good day."
Reggie stopped mid-sentence and stared at him.
Biscuit stopped mid-sentence and stared at him.
Mochi went back to his bowl.
"What?"
Biscuit smiled.
"I think the best part of the market was walking in it together."
Reggie nodded, very seriously, and went to sleep with his chin next to the peach.
Mochi pretended not to watch.
But he watched until the light went out.

card.front: The farmers market: one slow table, six new friends
card.back: Reggie: Fixed her morning. Biscuit: PEACHES. Mochi: Cheese. Acceptable. Good day.

facts: Farmers markets often allow leashed dogs
A dog's nose sits close to the height of market tables
